teamBuilding.label: Virtual team building activities

meta.title: 20 Virtual Team Building Activities Remote Teams Enjoy
meta.description: 20 virtual team building activities sorted by time: 5-minute starters, 30-minute games, monthly events and ideas that need no meeting at all.

teamBuilding.title: Virtual team building activities people actually enjoy.
teamBuilding.intro: Most virtual team building fails because it feels like one more meeting with games bolted on. What works is short, optional, easy to run and gives people something to talk about afterwards. Here are 20 activities sorted by how much time you have.

sections.title: What makes it work
body: Before picking an activity, get the format right. These five rules matter more than which game you choose.

items.title: Keep it short
items.body: Ten good minutes beat an hour nobody wanted. You can always run it again next week.

items.title: Make it optional
items.body: People join what they enjoy. Mandatory fun mostly teaches people to keep their camera off.

items.title: Run it in work hours
items.body: Evening events leave out parents, other time zones and anyone who needs the evening back.

items.title: Give everyone a way in
items.body: Mix activities for talkers and for quieter people: drawing, guessing and writing work as well as speaking.

items.title: Repeat what works
items.body: A small ritual every week does more than a big event every quarter.

sections.title: Five minutes, at the start of a meeting
body: No preparation, any team size. Use one to open a standup or a weekly meeting.

items.title: Two truths and a lie
items.body: One person says three things about themselves; the others guess which one is made up. Two or three people per meeting is plenty.

items.title: One thing on your desk
items.body: Everyone picks one object within reach and says why it's there. Easy for anyone, and it says a lot.

items.title: One-word check-in
items.body: Each person describes their week in one word. Follow up on the interesting ones later, not now.

items.title: This or that
items.body: The host reads pairs (coffee or tea, mountains or sea, early or late) and people answer in the chat at the same time.

items.title: Photo of the week
items.body: Each person shares one photo from their week, from their phone. No explanation needed unless they want to give one.

sections.title: Fifteen to thirty minutes
body: Something to put in the calendar every week or two, ideally on a Friday afternoon.

items.title: Pictionary on a shared whiteboard
items.body: One person draws a word on a whiteboard everyone can see while the others shout guesses. Keep a list of work words for an extra laugh.

items.title: Team trivia
items.body: Collect one surprising fact from each person beforehand, then quiz the team on who it belongs to.

items.title: Guess the song
items.body: Everyone sends the host one song they love. The host plays a few seconds of each and the team guesses whose it is.

items.title: Desert island picks
items.body: Each person names one book, one album and one food they'd take to a desert island, and the team argues about it.

items.title: Show and tell
items.body: One or two people a week show something they made, cook, grow or collect. People learn more about each other than in any game.

sections.title: An hour, once a month or a quarter
body: Bigger events need some planning or a small budget. Run them less often and make them count.

items.title: An online escape room
items.body: Several companies run hosted escape rooms over video. Split bigger teams into rooms and compare times at the end.

items.title: A class with a kit
items.body: Cooking, coffee or cocktail classes where everyone gets the same ingredients at home. Order early if your team is in several countries.

items.title: A game tournament
items.body: Free browser games like Gartic Phone, skribbl.io or Codenames online work well. Play in small groups, then a final.

items.title: A build day
items.body: Small teams build anything they like, work-related or not, and demo it at the end. It mixes people who never work together.

items.title: The quarter in review
items.body: Look back at what the team shipped, then hand out silly awards voted by everyone: best bug, best save, best meme.

sections.title: Without a meeting at all
body: Not everything needs a call. These run in a chat channel over a week and suit teams across time zones.

items.title: A photo challenge
items.body: A theme each week (your view, your lunch, something blue) and a channel to post in.

items.title: A kudos thread
items.body: One place to thank someone in public for something specific. Read the best ones out at the end of the month.

items.title: A recipe swap
items.body: Everyone shares one recipe from home. Collect them in a shared doc; it becomes the team cookbook.

items.title: A step challenge
items.body: Teams of three add up their daily steps. Keep it friendly and let people join with any kind of movement.

items.title: A book or podcast club
items.body: Pick one thing to read or listen to, discuss it in a thread, and meet once at the end if people want to.

sections.title: Make it a habit, not an event
body: The teams that feel closest rarely rely on big events. What they have is lots of small, unplanned moments: a quick word before a meeting, a question that turns into a chat, a song someone puts on.

In an office those happen by themselves. Remotely, they need a place where people can see each other and drop in without booking a call. Give your team that, and the activities above become the extra, not the only time people talk.

fit.title: Where TinyFloor fits
fit.body: TinyFloor is a virtual office your team walks around in. Pass someone and stop for a chat, put a song on the jukebox in the lounge, draw on the whiteboard for Pictionary, or meet in the meeting room for Friday drinks. It's free for up to 3 people, in the browser.

faq.q: What are good virtual team building activities for small teams?
faq.a: Short ones that need no preparation: two truths and a lie, one thing on your desk, Pictionary on a shared whiteboard or guess the song. Small teams can do something every week instead of a big event every quarter.

faq.q: How often should a remote team do team building?
faq.a: A five-minute starter in a weekly meeting and something longer once a month works for most teams. A small ritual done every week does more than a big event done rarely.

faq.q: How do you make virtual team building less awkward?
faq.a: Keep it short and optional, run it in work hours, give a clear host and rules, and choose activities where quieter people can draw, guess or write instead of perform.

faq.q: What free tools can we use?
faq.a: Gartic Phone, skribbl.io and Codenames online are free in the browser. A shared whiteboard covers drawing games, and a chat channel covers anything asynchronous. TinyFloor is free for up to 3 people.

meetingGames.label: Games for virtual meetings

meta.title: 15 Quick Games for Virtual Meetings (5 Minutes or Less)
meta.description: 15 quick games for virtual meetings that need no preparation: talking games, guessing games and drawing games that fit in five minutes.

meetingGames.title: Quick games for virtual meetings.
meetingGames.intro: A good meeting game takes five minutes, needs no preparation and works whether cameras are on or off. These 15 do, sorted by the kind of fun they are.

items.title: Pick a host
items.body: One person explains the rules, keeps time and moves things on. Rotate the job each week.

items.title: Set a timer
items.body: Five minutes means five minutes. Ending while it's still fun is how you get people to want it next time.

items.title: Nobody has to perform
items.body: Let people pass, answer in the chat or play with their camera off.

items.title: Would you rather
items.body: The host asks a choice between two options, everyone answers in one word, and two people explain theirs.

items.title: Hot takes
items.body: Someone shares a mild opinion (pineapple on pizza, tabs over spaces) and everyone rates it from 1 to 10.

items.title: Rose, thorn, bud
items.body: Each person shares something good, something hard and something they're looking forward to, in one sentence each.

items.title: One-word story
items.body: Go round the call, each adding one word to a story. It falls apart fast, which is the point.

items.title: Fortunately, unfortunately
items.body: Take turns adding a sentence to a story, alternating between good news and bad news.

items.title: Guess the desk
items.body: People send the host a photo of their desk beforehand; the team guesses whose is whose.

items.title: Pet or baby photo match
items.body: The same idea with photos of pets or of people as children. Always a favourite.

items.title: My week in emoji
items.body: Everyone posts three emoji that sum up their week in the chat; the others guess the story.

items.title: Guess the sound
items.body: The host plays short everyday sounds and people guess what they are. Sounds from around the house work best.

items.title: Twenty questions
items.body: One person thinks of something; the others ask yes-or-no questions until someone gets it.

items.title: Thirty-second drawing
items.body: Give a word, set a 30-second timer, and everyone draws it on a shared whiteboard at once.

items.title: Gartic Phone
items.body: Free in the browser: a drawing version of telephone where a sentence turns into something else entirely.

items.title: skribbl.io
items.body: Free online Pictionary with a private room. Add your own team words for inside jokes.

items.title: Sixty-second scavenger hunt
items.body: Name an object (something red, something older than you) and everyone races to show it on camera.

items.title: Five-question quiz
items.body: Five quick questions about the week, the product or the team. Answers in the chat; the fastest correct answer wins.

sections.title: How to run one well
body: Play at the start of the meeting, not the end, when people are fresh and nobody is rushing off. Keep the same game for a few weeks so nobody has to learn rules every time, then change it.
For big meetings, split into small groups of four to six. Games stop working when most people are watching instead of playing.

fit.title: Where TinyFloor fits
fit.body: In TinyFloor your team's meeting room is always there: join a meeting and your character walks in, no link to send. The shared whiteboard on the wall works for drawing games, and the floor stays open afterwards for whoever wants to keep chatting.

faq.q: What is a good five-minute game for a virtual meeting?
faq.a: Would you rather, hot takes or a thirty-second drawing on a shared whiteboard. They need no preparation and work with cameras on or off.

faq.q: What's the difference between an icebreaker and a meeting game?
faq.a: An icebreaker gets people talking about themselves, usually at the start of a new group. A meeting game is a short bit of fun for a team that already knows each other. Many of the games here work as both.

faq.q: How do you play games in a large virtual meeting?
faq.a: Split into groups of four to six, give each group the same game and a few minutes, then bring everyone back to share the best answer.

faq.q: Do we need special software?
faq.a: No. Most of these work on any video call with the chat. Gartic Phone and skribbl.io are free in the browser, and a shared whiteboard covers drawing games.

remoteCulture.label: Remote team culture

meta.title: How to Build Culture on a Remote Team: 9 Habits That Work
meta.description: How to build culture on a remote team: nine everyday habits that work, what to stop doing, and how to tell whether it's working.

remoteCulture.title: How to build culture on a remote team.
remoteCulture.intro: Culture is what people do every day when nobody is watching: how they ask for help, share news and disagree. A remote team loses the small moments that shape it in an office, so it has to make room for them on purpose, lightly and every day.

sections.title: What culture is without an office
body: In an office, a lot of culture happens by accident. You overhear how a senior colleague handles a tricky customer, you see who stays late before a launch, you go for lunch with someone from another team.
Remote work removes most of that. What's left is what people write, what they say in calls and what they choose to make visible. The good news is that all of it can be shaped by a few clear habits.

items.title: Write decisions down
items.body: Keep one place where decisions and their reasons live. New people learn how the team thinks by reading it.

items.title: Default to public channels
items.body: Ask questions where others can see and learn. Private messages are for private matters.

items.title: Make people visible
items.body: Show who's around, who's busy and who's free to talk, so asking for help doesn't feel like interrupting.

items.title: Keep a place to drop in
items.body: An always-open room or standing office hours where people can turn up without booking anything.

items.title: Run small rituals
items.body: A weekly demo, a Friday wins thread, a five-minute game. Small, regular and the same every week.

items.title: Give new people a buddy
items.body: Onboarding should be a person, not just a document: someone to ask the silly questions in the first month.

items.title: Celebrate in public
items.body: Thank people for specific things where the whole team can see. It shows what the team values.

items.title: Protect focus time
items.body: A good remote culture lets people go quiet for hours. Make 'busy' a respected status, not a warning sign.

items.title: Meet in person when you can
items.body: Once or twice a year, if the budget allows. It makes every call afterwards easier.

items.title: Mandatory fun
items.body: Required social events at awkward hours build resentment, not closeness.

items.title: Cameras on for everything
items.body: Video is useful for some conversations and tiring for all of them. Let people choose.

items.title: Tracking activity
items.body: Measuring keystrokes or online time tells people they aren't trusted, and trust is the whole point.

items.title: Meetings to stay connected
items.body: A daily all-hands to feel together usually feels like a chore. Give people a place to meet instead of a time.

sections.title: How to tell it's working
body: You won't find it in a survey score. Look for these instead:

items.title: New people ask questions in public
items.body: It means they feel safe not knowing something.

items.title: People help across teams
items.body: Without a ticket or a manager asking them to.

items.title: Small talk happens unprompted
items.body: Conversations start without a calendar invite.

items.title: People actually switch off
items.body: They take holidays and log off at the end of the day.

fit.title: Where TinyFloor fits
fit.body: TinyFloor gives a remote team a place to be together: a floor where you can see who's around, set a status, and walk over to talk when someone's free. It shows who's in and what status they choose, and nothing more: it doesn't track anyone's activity.

faq.q: Can a remote team have a strong culture?
faq.a: Yes. It just doesn't happen by accident. Teams that write decisions down, keep a place to drop in, run small rituals and celebrate in public often end up closer than teams in an office.

faq.q: What's the biggest challenge for remote team culture?
faq.a: Losing the small unplanned moments: overheard conversations, quick questions, lunch with someone new. A remote team needs a place where those can still happen.

faq.q: How do you make new hires feel part of a remote team?
faq.a: Give them a buddy, introduce them in a public channel, invite them to the team's rituals from day one and make it easy to see who's around to ask.

faq.q: How do you build culture across time zones?
faq.a: Lean on writing and asynchronous rituals, like a weekly thread or a photo challenge, and find an overlap of an hour or two for live moments. Rotate meeting times so the same people aren't always up late.

remoteCommunication.label: Remote team communication

meta.title: Remote Team Communication: When to Write and When to Talk
meta.description: A practical guide to remote team communication: when to write, when to talk, simple team rules and fixes for the most common problems.

remoteCommunication.title: Remote team communication: when to write, when to talk.
remoteCommunication.intro: Most communication problems on remote teams come from using the wrong mode: a long thread that should have been a two-minute call, or a meeting that should have been a message. Here's how to choose, and a few simple rules to agree as a team.

items.title: Someone will need it later
items.body: Decisions, how-tos and anything a new person will look for in three months.

items.title: It needs thought
items.body: Proposals and feedback get better when people can read twice and reply when ready.

items.title: People are in other time zones
items.body: Writing lets everyone take part in their own working hours.

items.title: It's a status update
items.body: Updates read in a minute take ten in a meeting.

items.title: A thread passes three replies
items.body: If it's still going back and forth, two minutes of talking will settle it.

items.title: Someone is blocked
items.body: Unblocking a teammate is worth an interruption. Walk over, look at it together and get them moving.

items.title: There's tension
items.body: Tone gets lost in text. Disagreements and difficult feedback go better out loud.

items.title: You're exploring ideas
items.body: Early brainstorming is faster in conversation. Write up what you decided afterwards.

sections.title: Simple rules to agree as a team
body: Write these down once and point new people to them. They prevent most of the friction.

items.title: Response times by channel
items.body: For example: chat within a few hours, email within a day, and a call for anything urgent.

items.title: One home for decisions
items.body: A channel or a doc where decisions are recorded, so they aren't lost in private messages.

items.title: Status means something
items.body: Busy means don't disturb unless it's urgent. Available means it's fine to walk over.

items.title: Every call ends in writing
items.body: Two lines in the right channel: what was decided and who does what.

items.title: No agenda, no meeting
items.body: A meeting without a purpose written in the invite can be declined.

items.title: Everything feels urgent
items.body: Agree what urgent means and which channel it uses. Everything else can wait for a reply.

items.title: Decisions get lost
items.body: Move them out of private messages into the decisions channel, every time.

items.title: Too many meetings
items.body: Replace status meetings with written updates and keep calls for decisions and problems.

items.title: People go quiet
items.body: Quiet people often don't want to interrupt. Make it easy to see when someone's free, and check in one to one.

fit.title: Where TinyFloor fits
fit.body: TinyFloor puts written and spoken communication side by side. Channels and messages stay in the team chat; when a thread gets long, you can see whether the person is free and walk over to talk. A status shows when someone is focused, so nobody has to guess.

faq.q: What are the best communication tools for remote teams?
faq.a: Most teams need four things: a chat for quick messages, a place for documents and decisions, video calls, and a way to see who's around. Many tools cover more than one; what matters is agreeing what each is for.

faq.q: Should remote teams work synchronously or asynchronously?
faq.a: Both. Write by default for updates and decisions, and talk live to unblock, resolve tension and explore ideas. Most teams need a few hours of overlap a day for the live part.

faq.q: How do you avoid too many meetings?
faq.a: Replace status meetings with written updates, require an agenda for every meeting, and make quick conversations easy, so people don't book a meeting for a two-minute question.

faq.q: How do you communicate across time zones?
faq.a: Default to writing, record decisions where everyone can find them, rotate live meeting times, and keep the overlap hours for the conversations that need them.

proximityChat.label: What is proximity chat?

meta.title: What Is Proximity Chat? How It Works in Games and at Work
meta.description: What proximity chat is, how it works, which games use it and how virtual offices use it so remote teams can talk by walking up to each other.

proximityChat.title: What is proximity chat?
proximityChat.intro: Proximity chat lets you talk to the people near you in a virtual space, and not to everyone else. It started in games, where it makes worlds feel alive, and is now how virtual offices let teams talk without meeting links.

sections.title: How proximity chat works
body: Every person has a position on a map, in a game world or on an office floor. Instead of everyone hearing everyone, the space decides who can talk: get close to someone and you can hear each other, move away and the conversation ends.
Some versions fade voices with distance, the way sound works in a room. Others connect you once you're next to someone, the way you'd walk up to a colleague's desk.

sections.title: Proximity chat in games
body: Games use it to make conversations part of the world. Some well-known examples:

items.title: Social deduction games
items.body: Mods for Among Us added proximity voice, so you only hear the players near you and can whisper plans.

items.title: Survival games
items.body: Rust and DayZ use proximity voice, so meeting a stranger means actually talking to them.

items.title: Co-op games
items.body: In Lethal Company, a teammate who wanders off becomes hard to hear, which is half the tension.

items.title: Sandbox games
items.body: Minecraft servers add proximity voice with mods, so a shared world feels like a real place.

sections.title: Proximity chat at work
body: Virtual offices use the same idea for remote teams. Your team shares a 2D floor, each person is a character, and you talk by moving next to someone instead of sending a meeting link.
It brings back what video calls lose: seeing who's around, quick questions and side conversations. Two people can talk in one corner while others work, the way they would in a real office.

items.title: Always-on spatial audio
items.body: Audio connects automatically when you're near someone and fades with distance. It feels lively, but you can be heard before you mean to be.

items.title: Walk up and call
items.body: Walking up to someone gives you a button to call them, and nothing is heard until you start the call. It's calmer and suits work better.

items.title: No meeting links
items.body: Talking is as easy as walking over, so small questions get asked.

items.title: Side conversations
items.body: Several conversations can happen at once in the same space.

items.title: Presence
items.body: You can see who's around before you interrupt anyone.

items.title: It needs a shared space
items.body: It only works if the team keeps the space open while they work.

fit.title: Where TinyFloor fits
fit.body: TinyFloor uses the walk-up style: walk your character up to a teammate and a call button appears beside them, so nobody is heard by accident. Groups meet in the meeting room. It runs in the browser and is free for up to 3 people.

faq.q: What does proximity chat mean?
faq.a: It means you can talk only to the people close to you in a virtual space. Move closer to someone to talk; move away and the conversation ends.

faq.q: Is proximity chat private?
faq.a: Only people near you can hear you, which is more private than a channel everyone is in. In the walk-up style, nothing is heard until you start a call.

faq.q: Which games have proximity chat?
faq.a: Rust, DayZ and Lethal Company have it built in, and mods add it to games like Among Us and Minecraft.

faq.q: Can you use proximity chat for work?
faq.a: Yes. Virtual offices like TinyFloor, Gather and SpatialChat use it so remote teams can talk by walking up to each other instead of scheduling calls.

bestVirtualOffice.title: The best virtual office software in 2026, honestly compared.
bestVirtualOffice.intro: A virtual office gives a remote team one place to be all day: you see who's around and talk by walking up to them, not by sending a link. Here are the nine worth looking at, what each costs and who each is for. We make TinyFloor, so we're not neutral; we say where each product is stronger than ours, and every price comes from its own pricing page, checked in October 2026.

sections.title: What a virtual office is
body: A virtual office is a shared 2D or 3D space where each person on the team has a character or a tile. The space stays open while people work, so you can see at a glance who's in, who's busy and who's in a call.

Conversations start the way they would in an office: you move next to someone and talk. Most virtual offices also have meeting rooms, screen sharing and chat, so a small team can use one for most of its day.

items.title: How it's priced
items.body: Most charge per person each month, which adds up as the team grows. A few charge per office or per space instead.

items.title: The free plan
items.body: Check the limits: how many people, how many hours a day and how long a meeting can last.

items.title: Browser or app
items.body: A browser office needs nothing installed, which matters for guests and new hires. A desktop app can feel smoother on a computer you own.

items.title: How a conversation starts
items.body: With spatial audio you're heard as soon as you're close. With walk-up calls nothing is heard until someone starts the call, which is calmer for work.

items.title: What you'll use every day
items.body: Calls, a meeting room, chat and screen sharing are what most teams use. Recordings, AI notes and map editors are useful to some teams, and usually cost more.

items.title: TinyFloor
items.detail: Free for 3 people · $19 a month for 10, $49 for 25
items.body: A pixel-art office in the browser, on desktop and mobile. Walk up to a teammate to start a video call, sit at a table to meet, with chat channels, screen sharing and a whiteboard. One price for the whole office, not per person. It has no recordings, AI notes or map editor, and offices top out at 25 people.

items.title: Gather
items.detail: No free plan · $12 a member a month billed yearly, $15 monthly
items.body: The best-known virtual office, with the most features: a custom office you design, recordings and transcription, Google Calendar, GitHub and Spotify integrations, and guests. It ended its free plan in 2025, so it's one of the more expensive choices for a small team.

items.title: SoWork
items.detail: Free for 10 members · Basic $5.40 a member a month billed yearly
items.body: A virtual office with meeting rooms, team chat and calendar integration. The free plan fits up to 10 members but limits meetings to 30 minutes and has no recordings. Premium, at $12 a member a month billed yearly, adds AI summaries, unlimited recordings and analytics.

items.title: Kumospace
items.detail: Free for 5 members · Business $16 a user a month
items.body: A polished space with spatial audio and desktop and mobile apps, popular for social events as well as offices. The free plan covers 5 members and one floor. It's among the more expensive for a team of 10 or more.

items.title: WorkAdventure
items.detail: Free for 10 people at once · Business €8 a user a month
items.body: An open-source pixel-art world you can host yourself, with maps you build in the Tiled editor. Good for technical teams and events that want full control. Setting up a custom map or your own server takes real work.

items.title: SpatialChat
items.detail: Free 2 hours a day for 12 · $5 a user a day, Business from $399 a month
items.body: Rooms with spatial audio and video bubbles, used a lot for events, classes and workshops. The free plan suits occasional sessions; a team that's in all day needs a Business plan.

items.title: Roam
items.detail: No free plan · $19.50 an active member a month
items.body: A desktop app for Mac and Windows that bundles a virtual office with meetings, chat, an AI assistant and webinars. You only pay for members who use it that month. It's a whole workplace suite, priced like one.

items.title: oVice
items.detail: Free version without support · $65 a month a space, billed yearly
items.body: A 2D office priced per space: Entry-S suits about 10 regular members, and Business Starter is $16 a user a month from 20 users. Strong in Japan and with larger companies. The free plan runs on a pre-release version without support.

items.title: Sococo
items.detail: No free plan · $13.49 a seat a month, billed yearly, 10 seats minimum
items.body: A bird's-eye floor plan of rooms rather than characters, with several screen shares at once. Each seat includes 500 meeting minutes a month. Built for companies that buy software by the year.

faq.a: No. Gather ended its free plan in 2025. It has a 30-day trial, then costs $12 a member a month billed yearly or $15 monthly.

faq.q: Do I need to install anything?
faq.a: Not for TinyFloor, Gather, SoWork, WorkAdventure, SpatialChat or oVice, which run in the browser. Roam is a desktop app, and Kumospace and Gather offer apps as well.

meta.title: Gather Pricing 2026: What a Team of 5, 10 or 25 Pays
meta.description: Gather costs $12 a member a month billed yearly or $15 monthly, with no free plan. What that comes to for teams of 5, 10, 25 and 50, and what the same team pays elsewhere.

gatherPricing.title: What does Gather cost?
gatherPricing.intro: Since September 2025, Gather charges for every member and has no free plan. Here is what that comes to for your team, worked out by size, and what the same team pays on other virtual offices. Prices are from Gather's own pricing and help pages, checked in October 2026.

sections.title: Gather's plans
body: Gather has one plan for most teams, Essential, and a Custom plan for large organisations.

items.title: Essential
items.body: $15 a member a month, or $12 billed yearly. It includes every Gather feature: a custom virtual office, unlimited meetings and chat, Google Calendar, GitHub and Spotify integrations, guests, and meeting recordings and transcriptions with monthly hour allowances.

items.title: Custom
items.body: Priced by Gather's sales team, for large teams that want custom onboarding and enterprise features.

items.title: Free trial
items.body: 30 days free, then Essential. There is no permanent free plan.

sections.title: What Gather costs by team size

head: Team
Billed monthly
Billed yearly, a month
A year, billed yearly
table.note: Gather charges for every member, whether or not they come into the office that day. Prices before tax.

sections.title: What changed in 2025
body: On September 15, 2025, Gather launched Gather 2.0 and moved both the new and the original version to pricing per member: $15 a member a month, or $12 billed yearly. Before, teams paid for how many people were in the office at the same time.
The free plan ended for both versions. Teams already paying could lock in their old price before the change. For a small team that used Gather for free, this was the moment it started to cost money.

sections.title: The same team elsewhere
body: Here is what the same teams pay a month on other virtual offices, on the cheapest plan that fits them.

head: Team
Gather, billed yearly
TinyFloor
SoWork Basic, billed yearly
Kumospace Business
table.note: From each product's own pricing page in October 2026, before tax. SoWork's free plan also covers up to 10 members, with meetings capped at 30 minutes, and WorkAdventure's covers up to 10 people at once.

items.title: You want to design your office
items.body: Gather lets you lay out floors, rooms and objects. Most alternatives give you a ready-made office.

items.title: You need recordings and transcripts
items.body: Essential includes them, with hour allowances each month.

items.title: Your day runs on Google Calendar and GitHub
items.body: Gather's integrations show your status and activity in the office.

items.title: When it isn't
items.body: If your team mostly needs to see who's around, talk and meet, you're paying for features you won't use, every month, for every person.

fit.title: Where TinyFloor fits
fit.body: TinyFloor keeps the core of what Gather does, an office you walk around in where you talk by walking up to someone, with a meeting room, chat and screen sharing. It costs $19 a month for up to 10 people and $49 for up to 25, one price for the whole office, and it's free for up to 3. It has no recordings, transcription or office editor, so if you rely on those, Gather is the better fit.

faq.q: How much does Gather cost?
faq.a: $15 a member a month billed monthly, or $12 a member a month billed yearly, on the Essential plan. Larger organisations can ask for a Custom plan.

faq.q: Does Gather have a free plan?
faq.a: No. Gather ended its free plan in September 2025. It offers a 30-day free trial instead.

faq.q: How much does Gather cost for 10 people?
faq.a: $150 a month billed monthly, or $120 a month billed yearly ($1,440 a year).

faq.q: What is a cheaper alternative to Gather?
faq.a: TinyFloor is $19 a month for up to 10 people and free for up to 3. SoWork's Basic plan is $5.40 a member a month billed yearly, and its free plan covers 10 members with 30-minute meetings.
